thread.title_full: Gov. Ron DeSantis honors Ben Franklin with new statue on Constitution Day - NewsBreak

author: James Call
title: Gov. Ron DeSantis honors Ben Franklin with new statue on Constitution Day - NewsBreak
text:
By James Call ,
11 hours ago Gov. Ron DeSantis unveiled a statue of Benjamin Franklin on the Franklin County courthouse grounds Sept. 17, and quoted a passage from Franklin’s Poor Richard’s Almanac as a foundational principle for elected officials.
DeSantis, who taught U.S. history for a year after graduating from Yale in 2001, noted the unveiling was taking place on Constitution Day, the 238th anniversary of the signing of the U. S. Constitution in Philadelphia.
The nearly six-foot bronze statue of a standing Ben Franklin holding a copy of the U.S. Constitution is at 33 Market Street in downtown Apalachicola. It's now the second of five of the Founding Fathers that will be installed at their county namesakes over the next year.
The public art displays are part of Florida’s America 250FL campaign , commemorating the 250th anniversary of the signing of the U.S. Constitution.
Before an audience of local officials, residents and media, DeSantis recounted Franklin’s influence as a member of the committee that wrote the Constitution and how he counseled other delegates of the need to “hang together or assuredly we shall all hang separately.”
The governor also repeated a famous quote attributed to Franklin, said to have uttered it as he left the Constitutional Convention in 1787, after being asked what kind of government had been created: "A republic, if you can keep it.”
As he did two months ago when a statue of Thomas Jefferson was debuted in Jefferson County, DeSantis expounded, without notes and at length, a detailed history of the challenges faced by the Founding Fathers and Franklin’s role in resolving them and his influence on society.
“I don’t know how he did all the stuff that he did,” DeSantis said.
DeSantis praised Franklin as writer, philosopher Not only was Franklin an effective statesman and diplomat, DeSantis said, Franklin also was “flying the kite, you know, with lightning strikes. He's doing things on bifocals. He did a stove. He founded the University of Pennsylvania.”
DeSantis then praised Franklin as a writer and philosopher, saying the rules and principles for life outlined in Poor Richard’s Almanac, published in 1758, still ring true today.
“One of the things he said is ‘well done is better than well said,’ and ultimately that’s something I’ve certainly tried to live by. Words can be meaningful, but deeds are ultimately the most powerful. Don’t tell me what you’re going to do. Show me that you’re actually going to get it done. If everyone in elected office stood by what Franklin said, we'd have a lot more productivity around the country than we do now,” DeSantis said.
Afterwards, in an exchange with reporters, DeSantis referred to the Charlie Kirk assassination to call attention to the importance of free speech and debate as fundamental American principles. The governor also praised CFO Blaise Ingolia’s efforts to audit local government for wasteful spending and promoted his goal to eliminate property taxes.
The statue was made by Austin Weishel , a Colorado sculptor and former firefighter and EMT, according to his website. Future founding father statues are scheduled to be installed in Madison, Hamilton, and Monroe counties.
(This story was updated to add new information.)
James Call can be reached at jcall@tallahassee.com. Follow on him Twitter: @CallTallahassee .
